teacherGuide.overview: Defines work and power with a bucket-carrying example, derives the horsepower from James Watt’s comparison with a horse, links simple machines to reduced force, and shows watts and kilowatts in Ghanaian life.
learningGoals: Calculate work done using work = force × distance.
Calculate power using power = work ÷ time, and convert watts to kilowatts.
Explain how a simple machine reduces the force needed without reducing the work.
Describe the energy changes in a fuel engine and in an electric motor.

beforeReading: Ask: What do you mean when you say you have “worked hard”? Collect answers, then compare them with the scientific meaning after Page 1.
whileReading: Pause on Page 2 and have two volunteers time each other climbing a short flight of steps. Who is more powerful?
afterReading: Survey the power ratings (in watts) on five appliances at home or school and rank them.
discussion: A ramp makes loading easier, yet the total work is no less. How can both be true?
reflection: Which simple machines did you use today without noticing?

mathsExtension.task: A loader pushes a drum with a force of 300 N along a plank 4 m long. How much work is done?
He takes 8 seconds. What is his power?
A corn-mill engine is rated at 8 horsepower. What is that in kilowatts?
How many 2,000 W kettles could Akosombo’s 1,020 MW supply at once?

support: Give a formula card: work (J) = force (N) × distance (m); power (W) = work (J) ÷ time (s).
stretch: Measure your own power: find your weight in newtons, climb a measured flight of steps, time it, and calculate your power in watts and in horsepower.

factCheck.claim: One horsepower is about 750 watts; Akosombo Dam has an installed capacity of 1,020 megawatts.
factCheck.explanation: Arithmetic checked (15,000 kg × 10 N/kg × 0.3 m ÷ 60 s = 750 W; mechanical horsepower is 745.7 W). Akosombo’s installed capacity is 1,020 MW.
factCheck.reference: Volta River Authority (VRA) Akosombo Hydroelectric Plant specifications; SI / imperial unit conversion tables.
